evidence.limitation: Small groups and a single cell line.

bench.question: Can a smaller particle with a softer surface reach deeper into tissue that is packed with fibres?
bench.approach: The authors made two particle sizes, tracked them with fluorescence, and compared penetration depth in sections of treated tumours.
bench.model: Mice carrying tumours grown from one human cell line, eight animals per group.
bench.result: Placeholder numbers: the small particle reached a mean depth of 120 micrometres against 45 for the large one, and tumours shrank 38 percent more.
bench.limitations: One cell line, no survival endpoint, and a short follow-up. The comparison drug dose was not a clinical dose.
bench.meaning: If the depth gain holds in models that better copy human tissue, it could change how particles are designed for dense tumours.

bench.question: Does one night of shorter sleep change measured attention the next day?
bench.approach: A crossover design: each volunteer completed the task after normal sleep and after restricted sleep, in random order.

method.title: Measure particle size and charge before every experiment
method.gist: Two quick measurements, size and surface charge, tell you whether a particle batch is the one you think it is.
method.useWhen: Before dosing cells or animals, and after any change to how particles are made or stored.

steps.title: Dilute the sample
steps.text: Dilute to the concentration the source protocol gives, in the same buffer you will use for the experiment.

steps.title: Measure size
steps.text: Run the size measurement in at least three repeats and record the average and the spread.

steps.title: Measure surface charge
steps.text: Measure the zeta potential in the same buffer and note the pH.

steps.title: Compare with the last batch
steps.text: Reject a batch that differs from your recorded range, and write down why.

pitfalls: Salt-rich buffers can change the reading, so always report the buffer.
method.safety: Placeholder steps only. Follow your institution's rules for handling nanomaterials, lasers and biological samples, and ask your safety officer if unsure.

terms.def: A measure of the electric charge near a particle's surface, which affects whether particles clump.

learn.question: What is the EPR effect?
learn.answer: Some tumours have leaky blood vessels and poor drainage, so small particles can slip in and stay there. This is called the enhanced permeability and retention effect.
learn.analogy: Think of a garden hose with holes and a blocked drain: water gets out and stays in the flower bed.
body: Normal vessels are tight, so most particles stay in the blood. Many tumours grow vessels fast and badly, leaving gaps that particles of about 10 to 200 nanometres can pass through.
The effect varies a lot between tumour types and between patients. Dense tissue around a tumour can block particles even when the vessels leak, which is one reason it works less well in some cancers.

diagram.caption: Placeholder cross section: particles leave through gaps and are slow to leave the tissue.

terms.def: How easily something passes through a barrier.
